sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Community acquired Pneumonia (CAP) is defined as an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma that is acquired outside a hospital or healthcare setting. It typically presents with symptoms of acute infection, accompanied by the presence of an acute infiltrate on a chest radiograph or auscultatory findings (such as altered breath sounds and/or localized rales). To diagnose CAP, at least one systemic feature (either a symptom complex of sweating, fevers, shivers, aches and pains and/or temperature of 38°C or more) must be present, with no alternative explanation for the illness. Community acquired pneumonia remains a disease with high mortality if not recognized timely and correctly managed.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.body: To provide accurate and update information to care providers who manage CAP cases in the hospital so that diagnosis and appropriate management of CAP are done timely and correctly.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.body: To improve outcome of patients presenting at King Faisal Hospital with community acquired pneumonia.

sections.heading: Rationale
sections.body: Failure to diagnose CAP timely or administering the wrong antibiotics, can have serious and potentially fatal consequences. This guideline provides recommendations to prevent delay or incorrect treatment, aiming to reduce hospital stay and minimize complications from pneumonia.

sections.heading: Scope of Guideline
sections.body: This guideline is intended for all healthcare provides managing adult or adolescent patients with community-acquired pneumonia. This can be in the general outpatient department, internal medicine departments and Accident & Emergency department. The guideline applies to all adult or adolescent patients presenting with CAP that are seen in King Faisal Hospital, both inpatients and outpatients.

sections.heading: Competencies Required
sections.body: Every medical doctor working in the mentioned areas where patients with CAP are managed has access to the guidelines and is competent to apply them.

sections.heading: Definition of Key Terms
bullets: CAP: Community Acquired Pneumonia
COPD: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
CURB-65: scoring system used to assess the severity of pneumonia based on 5 criteria: confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and age
HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
ICU: Intensive Care Unit
MRSA: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus
PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index Score
PO: per os
IV: intravenous
OD: once daily
BID: bis in die, twice a day
TDS: ter die sumendum, three times a day
QID: quater in die, four times a day

sections.heading: Assessment of Patients - Patient History
bullets: Symptoms of an acute lower respiratory tract illness: cough, sputum production, shortness of breath, chest pain.
Systemic signs: fevers, shivering, sweating.

Co-morbidities: COPD, Asthma, Diabetes Mellitus, Chronic Kidney Disease, Congestive Heart Failure, Coronary Artery disease, malignancy, asplenia, chronic neurological diseases and chronic liver diseases.
Smoking and alcohol abuse.
HIV status.
Recent (last 3 months) antibiotic use.
Recent hospitalization (last 3 months).
Tuberculosis infection / treatment in the past.

sections.heading: Assessment of Patients - Physical Examination
bullets: Vital signs: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, blood pressure, heart rate.
Inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation of chest.

sections.heading: Assessment of Patients - Etiology
sections.body: Organisms commonly associated with pneumonia are listed below.
bullets: Bacterial pathogens: Streptococcus pneumonia, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphyloccus aureus, Haemophilus influenza, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Group A Streptococci, Enterobacterales.
Atypical non-zoonotic bacterial pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella spp., Chlamydia pneumoniae.
Atypical zoonotic bacterial pathogens: Chlamydophila psittaci (psittacosis), Coxiella burnettii (Q fever).
Bronchiectasis or CF: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis can also present as CAP.
Viral pathogens: Influenza, SARS-CoV-2, other coronaviruses, rhinoviruses, parainfluenza viruses, adenoviruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus.
Pathogens related to CAP in immunocompromised patients are Burkholderia, fungi, P. jirovecii, Nocardia species.

sections.heading: Assessment of Patients - Diagnostics
bullets: Chest X-ray (CXR) is recommended as primary radiographic imaging. Expected findings include lobar consolidation, cavitary lesions, and interstitial pattern. In cases with high suspicion and inconclusive CXR, an additional chest CT is suggested. Compare with previous images if available.
Full blood count.
C-reactive protein.
Procalcitonin in patients who need admission.
Urea, creatinine and electrolytes as part of severity assessment.
Arterial blood gasses in patients with severe pneumonia.
COVID-19 rapid diagnostic test or PCR when findings are suggestive of viral pneumonia.
Blood culture (2 bottles for adults) in patients who need admission.

Sputum culture can be valuable in certain settings, including in hospitalized patients with severe symptoms, and when patients have a history of MRSA, Pseudomonas or Enterobacterales. It is not recommended as a routine investigation for CAP in the outpatient setting.
HIV screening in severe pneumonia patients.

In cases of severe pneumonia, rapid tests for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, along with respiratory virus panel PCR tests (including influenza), can be requested based on their availability.

sections.heading: Decision to Hospitalise Patients
sections.body: Not all patients with pneumonia require hospital admission. A risk-assessment should be performed for all patients with CAP to decide which patient can safely be managed at home. Main decision is based on severity of the disease. Other important considerations are the patient's socio-economic status and home circumstances.

sections.heading: Severity of Illness Assessment - Overview
sections.body: A number of severity of illness assessment tools have been developed to assist clinicians in assessing the severity of community-acquired pneumonia. Assessment of the severity of infection is important since it will determine appropriate site of care, microbiological work-up and empiric antibiotic treatment. The Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) recommended in 2019 using the PSI score over CURB-65 score to determine which patient can be safely treated as an outpatient.

sections.heading: Severity of Illness Assessment - PSI Score Risk Classes
bullets: Patients with CAP and scores of <50 (class 1) and 51-70 (class 2) are thought to be mild and potentially suitable for management at home.
Patients with scores of 71-90 (class 3) are considered moderately ill and need to be observed in hospital initially.
Patients with scores of > 91 (class 4 & 5) are thought to be severely ill, and need consideration for admission to a high-care or even intensive care unit.

sections.heading: Severity of Illness Assessment - Other Scores
bullets: Other scores, such as CURB-65, are less accurate, but could be used because of its simplicity and do not require the measurement of the urea level.

None of the scoring systems replace clinical assessment. Important additional factors, such as socioeconomic deprivation and co-morbidity, must influence the decision on hospitalization and treatment.
The PES score was developed in 2015 to predict the microbiological etiology of CAP caused by PES pathogens.
Patients are at risk for MRSA, multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas if: Hospitalization AND IV antibiotics in the last 90 days, or PES score ≥ 5.

sections.heading: Severity of Illness Assessment - ICU Admission Criteria
sections.body: In addition to the tables mentioned above, the ATS/IDSA also give recommendations on identifying patients who should be admitted to ICU for intensive monitoring and treatment. Patients requiring ICU-level care are:
bullets: Patients with hypotension requiring vasopressors or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation.
Patients with three or more of the following (minor) criteria, of course assessed on individual base:
Blood urea nitrogen ≥ 20 mg per dL (7.14 mmol per L).
Confusion or disorientation.
Core temperature < 36°C.
Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation.
Multilobar infiltrates.
Partial pressure of oxygen/fraction of inspired oxygen ratio ≤ 250.
Platelet count < 100,000 per µL (100x10^9 per L).
Respiratory rate ≥ 30 breaths per minute.
White blood cell count < 4,000 per µL (4.00x10^9 per L) due to infection alone (i.e., not chemotherapy induced).

sections.heading: Therapy and Follow-up - Supportive Therapy
bullets: Patient is given explanation about the diagnosis, prognosis and the therapy he/she will receive.
Analgesics and rehydration are started when indicated.
Oxygen therapy: up to 5L/min via nasal cannula; 6-10L/min via simple non face mask; more than 10L/min via non-rebreathing face mask or high-flow nasal cannula.

sections.heading: Empirical Antibiotic Therapy - Outpatients
bullets: Treatment options for previously healthy outpatients; no antibiotic use in past 3 months: Amoxicillin 1 gm PO every 8 hours for 5-7 days OR Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 625 mg po every 8 hours or 1 gram PO every 12 hours for 5-7 days OR Doxycycline 100mg PO every 12 hours for 7 days PLUS: Azithromycin 500 mg PO daily for 3 days.

Outpatients with comorbidities or antibiotic use in past three months: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 1 g PO BID for 5-7 days + Azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily for 3 days OR Third generation cephalosporin (such as cefixim 400 mg PO daily or 200 mg PO BID) for 5-7 days + Azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily for 3 days OR Amoxicillin-clavulanate 1 g PO BID + Clarithromycin 500 mg PO BID for 5-7 days.

Penicillin allergy: Doxycycline 100 mg PO every 12 hours for 7 days OR Levofloxacin* 750 mg PO OD (5 days) or moxifloxacin* 400 mg PO OD (5-7 days) (*Note: Fluoroquinolones should be avoided in patients with suspected TB).
If previous colonization with MRSA or Pseudomonas or high risk for multidrug-resistant organisms: empirically cover and total treatment will be 7-14 days.

sections.heading: Empirical Antibiotic Therapy - Inpatients
bullets: Beta-lactam antibiotics as intravenous ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for 5-7 days PLUS azithromycin 500 mg oral daily for 3-5 days.
In case of penicillin allergy: cephalosporins or respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin) are options.

In patients with severe pneumonia who have a history of prior antibiotic exposure, piperacillin-tazobactam is occasionally chosen as the initial treatment. This decision is always made in consultation with an infectious diseases specialist or pulmonologist.

Previous colonization with MRSA or pseudomonas in previous year OR high risk based on PES-score: MRSA: 3rd generation cephalosporin (7 days) + vancomycin + macrolide. Pseudomonas: Piperacillin-tazobactam / cefepime (7-14 days) + macrolide. Enterobacteriaceae: piperacillin-tazobactam / cefepime (7-10 days) + macrolide.
The American Thoracic Society (ATS)/Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines recommended that patients with CAP should be treated for a minimum of five days.

Before stopping therapy, the patient should be afebrile for 48 to 72 hours, breathing without supplemental oxygen (unless required for pre-existing disease), and have no more than one clinical instability factor (defined as heart rate >100 beats/minute, respiratory rate >24 breaths/minute, and SBP ≤90 mmHg).

sections.heading: Therapy and Follow-up - Special Considerations
bullets: Aspiration pneumonia. The 2019 American Thoracic Society (ATS) and Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines on CAP and the 2023 ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines for the management of severe community-acquired pneumonia guidelines recommend against routinely adding anaerobic coverage for patients with (suspected) aspiration pneumonia.
Corticosteroids are not recommended as adjunctive therapy for treatment of non-severe CAP.

However, given the potential beneficial effect on length of hospital stay and 28-day mortality, the use of corticosteroids is now recommended in patients with severe CAP who meet one of the following criteria: mechanical ventilation with PEEP > 5 cm water; high-flow oxygen with a FiO2 > 50% and PaO2:FiO2 ratio < 300; nonrebreathing mask with PaO2: FiO2 ratio < 300; PSI class V and the absence of relative contraindication (e.g. history suggesting aspiration, pneumonia caused by influenza).

sections.heading: Patients' follow-up and complications
bullets: Clinical response is expected within 48 hours otherwise there is a need to reconsider the therapy.
Shifting from IV to oral takes place when patients improve and can take oral therapy.
Complications are to be looked for and managed (empyema, meningitis, septicemia, shock).
After hospital discharge, routine use of follow-up chest imaging in adults with CAP who are improving after the start of antibiotic treatment is not recommended, unless there are complications.
Patients at high risk of lung cancer should benefit from a chest CT scan 4-8 weeks after discharge.
